analysis.one_liner: Guarantees garment workers hourly pay instead of piece-rate wages and registers manufacturers with labor officials.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee; no hearing or vote has been scheduled as of mid-September 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would end piece-rate pay in the garment industry — where workers are paid per item sewn rather than by the hour, a system often used to pay far below minimum wage in practice. Instead, employers would have to pay a guaranteed hourly wage. It would also require garment manufacturers and contractors to register with the Department of Labor, giving regulators a list of who is producing clothing and for whom.
analysis.who_benefits: Garment workers, many of them immigrants, who today can be paid by the piece and end up earning less than minimum wage when factories are slow or quotas are steep. Hourly pay makes their earnings predictable and easier to enforce, and the registration requirement makes it easier for the Department of Labor to find and inspect the factories actually doing the work.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Garment workers, many of them immigrants

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits employers in the garment industry from paying employees by piece rate, replacing per-item pay with an hourly wage [S1].
Requires garment manufacturers and contractors to register with the Department of Labor, creating a public record of who is producing apparel [S1].

analysis.who_pays: Garment manufacturers and contractors, who would lose the piece-rate system they use to control labor costs, and would take on new registration paperwork. Small shops with thin margins would feel the compliance burden most, and some may pass costs up the supply chain to brands or shift work overseas.

drawbacks.text: Federal wage law already requires employers who use piece rates to top up pay to at least minimum wage; this bill goes further and bans the system outright, which removes a flexible pay arrangement some workers and shops have used, even if it is also the mechanism most associated with subminimum earnings [S1].
Registration requirements and the loss of piece-rate pay add costs for small apparel contractors, and the industry has historically argued such rules push production to other countries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — a guaranteed hourly wage for workers in an industry with a long, documented history of subminimum piece-rate pay — is real and targeted at the practices that cause the harm. The main costs fall on manufacturers and contractors as compliance and labor-cost changes, and the bill's design (as far as the title shows) does not include provisions addressing what happens to small shops or to competition from abroad. On balance the burden falls on employers who currently benefit from the piece-rate system.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on September 14, 2026 and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it currently sits with no hearing or vote scheduled [S3].

narrative.text: Introduced in the House on September 14, 2026 [S1].
Referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, which is its only committee action so far [S3].
It has eight cosponsors, all Democrats, in addition to the sponsor [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No outcome yet. The bill is at the start of the process, and garment employers' current pay arrangements remain untouched while it sits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, nobody; the bill is pending

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban piece-rate pay in the garment industry and require manufacturer registration with the Department of Labor.

for.name: Eight Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Added their names in support of the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all eight cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican cosponsors appear as of referral, and the bill's fate rests with the Republican-led House Education and Workforce Committee [S2].

industries.note: The bill ends their ability to pay by the piece and requires them to register with the Department of Labor, raising guaranteed labor costs. Their savings under the current system come from pay arrangements that can leave workers below minimum wage, so their interest runs against the workers this bill protects.

analysis.trajectory: With no cosponsors from the House majority, no committee action beyond the initial referral, and the Congress ending in January 2027, the bill is likely to sit in committee without a hearing or a vote — the same path similar garment-worker pay bills have followed in recent Congresses.
